### Summary ###

Solution found with answer: \boxed{
\begin{cases}

### Detailed Solution ###

Summary**

**a. Verdict**  
I have obtained a complete solution.  
For every integer \(n\ge 3\) the admissible numbers of sunny lines are  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{cases}
\{0,1,3\}, & n=3,\\[2mm]
\{0,1\},   & n\ge 4 .
\end{cases}}
\]

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Notation.**  
   \[
   S_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^{2}\mid a\ge1,\;b\ge1,\;a+b\le n+1\},
   \qquad |S_n|=\dfrac{n(n+1)}2 .
   \tag{1}
   \]

2. **Sunny‑line bound.**  
   If a sunny line has reduced slope \(\dfrac pq\) with \(|p|,|q|\ge1\) and
   \((p,q)\neq(1,-1),(-1,1)\), then any two lattice points on it differ by a
   multiple of the vector \((q,p)\); consequently it contains at most  

   \[
   \Big\lfloor\frac{n+1}{2}\Big\rfloor
   \tag{2}
   \]

   points of \(S_n\).

3. **Columns.**  
   For a fixed abscissa \(a\;(1\le a\le n)\) the set  

   \[
   C_a=\{(a,b)\in S_n\}
   \]

   contains exactly  

   \[
   h_a=n+1-a
   \tag{3}
   \]

   points (the *\(a\)-th column*).  
   A sunny line meets each column in **at most one** point.

4. **Exchange Lemma.**  
   Let a family \(\mathcal L\) of \(n\) distinct lines cover \(S_n\) and contain
   exactly \(k\) sunny lines.  
   Replace every non‑sunny line that is not vertical by a vertical line
   through the leftmost column that is still uncovered.  
   Because a non‑vertical non‑sunny line meets each column in at most one
   point, this replacement never increases the number of uncovered points and
   does not change the number of sunny lines.  
   Hence we may **assume that all \(n-k\) non‑sunny lines are vertical** and
   that they are the lines  

   \[
   x=1,\;x=2,\dots ,x=n-k .
   \tag{4}
   \]

5. **The remaining triangle.**  
   After fixing the vertical lines (4) the uncovered part of \(S_n\) is  

   \[
   T_k=\bigl\{(a,b)\mid n-k+1\le a\le n,\;1\le b\le n+1-a\bigr\},
   \]

   a right‑angled triangular set consisting of the last \(k\) columns.
   Its cardinality is  

   \[
   |T_k|=\sum_{j=1}^{k}j=\frac{k(k+1)}2 .
   \tag{5}
   \]

   In each of these \(k\) columns a sunny line can contribute at most one
   point, therefore the \(k\) sunny lines can cover at most \(k^{2}\) points
   of \(T_k\).  Since \(\frac{k(k+1)}2\le k^{2}\) for every \(k\ge1\), the
   counting (5) does **not** forbid any value of \(k\); a finer geometric
   obstruction is needed.

6. **Geometric obstruction for \(k\ge2\) when \(n\ge4\).**  
   The two right‑most columns of \(T_k\) are  

   \[
   C_{n-1}=\{(n-1,1),(n-1,2)\},\qquad
   C_{n}   =\{(n,1)\}.
   \]

   Any sunny line can contain at most one of the three points
   \((n-1,1),(n-1,2),(n,1)\):
   * \((n-1,1)\) and \((n,1)\) are on a horizontal line (slope \(0\));
   * \((n-1,2)\) and \((n,1)\) are on a line of slope \(-1\);
   * \((n-1,1)\) and \((n-1,2)\) are on a vertical line (slope \(\infty\)).
   All three possibilities are forbidden for a sunny line.
   Consequently **each sunny line can cover at most one of these three points**.

   The set \(T_k\) always contains these three points (they belong to the
   last two columns, which are present as soon as \(k\ge2\)).  
   Hence at least three sunny lines are required to cover them.
   Therefore a configuration with \(k\ge2\) sunny lines cannot exist when
   \(n\ge4\) (because we would need at least three sunny lines but only
   \(k\) sunny lines are available).

7. **The case \(n=3\).**  
   For \(n=3\) the set \(S_3\) consists of six points.  
   The three lines  

   \[
   L_{1}:y=x,\qquad
   L_{2}:y=-\frac12x+\frac52,\qquad
   L_{3}:y=-2x+5
   \]

   are all sunny and together contain the six points; hence \(k=3\) is
   attainable.  
   The obstruction of step 6 does not apply because the “right‑most two
   columns’’ coincide (there are only three columns in total).  
   A direct inspection shows that \(k=2\) is impossible: the three points
   \((2,1),(2,2),(3,1)\) force the same argument as in step 6, leaving only
   one sunny line to cover three points, which cannot be done.

8. **Existence for the admissible values.**  

   *\(k=0\).*  The \(n\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n\) are all non‑sunny
   and cover every point of \(S_n\).

   *\(k=1\).*  Use the \(n-1\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n-1\).  
   The only uncovered point is \((n,1)\); the line through \((n,1)\) and
   \((1,2)\) has slope \(-\dfrac1{\,n-1\,}\neq0,\infty,-1\), hence it is
   sunny.  Thus exactly one sunny line is used.

   *\(n=3,\;k=3\).*  The three sunny lines displayed in step 7 cover all
   points of \(S_3\).

   No other values of \(k\) are possible by the impossibility proved in
   steps 6 and 7.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Detailed Solution**

Let  

\[
S_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^{2}\mid a\ge1,\;b\ge1,\;a+b\le n+1\},
\qquad |S_n|=\frac{n(n+1)}2 .
\tag{1}
\]

A line is called **sunny** iff its slope is different from \(0\), \(\infty\) and
\(-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A bound for a sunny line

Write a sunny line as \(y=mx+c\) with reduced rational slope
\(m=p/q\;(q>0,\;(p,q)=1)\) and \((p,q)\neq(1,-1),(-1,1)\).
If \((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\in S_n\) lie on the line then  

\[
y_2-y_1=m(x_2-x_1)=\frac pq\,(x_2-x_1),
\]

hence \(p\mid (y_2-y_1)\) and \(q\mid (x_2-x_1)\).
Thus all lattice points of the line are of the form  

\[
(x_0,y_0)+t\,(q,p),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z .
\tag{2}
\]

Inside the triangle \(S_n\) we have \(|x-x_0|\le n-1\) and
\(|y-y_0|\le n-1\); consequently  

\[
|t|\le\frac{n-1}{\max\{|p|,|q|\}} .
\]

Because a sunny line is not parallel to the axes nor to \(x+y=0\),
\(\max\{|p|,|q|\}\ge2\); therefore a sunny line contains at most  

\[
1+\Big\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\Big\rfloor
=\Big\lfloor\frac{n+1}{2}\Big\rfloor
\tag{3}
\]

points of \(S_n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Columns of \(S_n\)

For a fixed integer \(a\;(1\le a\le n)\) define  

\[
C_a=\{(a,b)\in S_n\}.
\]

From the definition of \(S_n\) we obtain  

\[
|C_a|=h_a=n+1-a .
\tag{4}
\]

Thus the heights of the columns are  

\[
h_1=n,\;h_2=n-1,\dots ,h_n=1 .
\]

A sunny line meets each column in **at most one** point, because two points
with the same abscissa would differ by a vector \((0,\Delta b)\), contradicting
(2) unless the line were vertical (non‑sunny).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Reduction to vertical non‑sunny lines  

Assume we have a family \(\mathcal L\) of \(n\) distinct lines covering
\(S_n\) and containing exactly \(k\) sunny lines (\(0\le k\le n\)).
Let the remaining \(n-k\) lines be non‑sunny.

A non‑sunny line is either vertical, horizontal or of slope \(-1\).
Both horizontal and slope \(-1\) lines intersect each column in **exactly one**
point (if the column is tall enough).  
Consequently, if a non‑vertical non‑sunny line is replaced by a vertical line
through the leftmost column that is still uncovered, the set of uncovered
points does not increase, and the number of sunny lines stays unchanged.
Repeating this replacement we obtain a new covering with the same numbers
\(n\) and \(k\) in which **all non‑sunny lines are vertical**.

Hence we may (and shall) assume that the non‑sunny lines are precisely  

\[
x=1,\;x=2,\dots ,x=n-k .
\tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The uncovered triangle  

After fixing the vertical lines (5) the points that are still uncovered form  

\[
T_k=\bigl\{(a,b)\mid n-k+1\le a\le n,\;1\le b\le n+1-a\bigr\},
\]

i.e. the last \(k\) columns of the original triangle.
A direct count gives  

\[
|T_k|=\sum_{j=1}^{k}j=\frac{k(k+1)}2 .
\tag{6}
\]

Each of the \(k\) sunny lines can meet each of these \(k\) columns in at most
one point; therefore the sunny lines can cover at most \(k^{2}\) points of
\(T_k\).  Since \(\frac{k(k+1)}2\le k^{2}\) for all \(k\ge1\), the
cardinality (6) does not by itself forbid any value of \(k\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Impossibility of two or more sunny lines when \(n\ge4\)

Assume \(k\ge2\) and \(n\ge4\).
The set \(T_k\) always contains the two right‑most columns

\[
C_{n-1}=\{(n-1,1),(n-1,2)\},\qquad
C_{n}   =\{(n,1)\}.
\tag{7}
\]

Consider the three points listed in (7).  
Any line that contains two of them has one of the forbidden slopes:

* \((n-1,1)\) and \((n,1)\) lie on a horizontal line (slope \(0\));
* \((n-1,2)\) and \((n,1)\) lie on a line of slope \(-1\);
* \((n-1,1)\) and \((n-1,2)\) lie on a vertical line (slope \(\infty\)).

Hence **no sunny line can contain more than one of the three points**.
Since the three points must all be covered, at least three sunny lines are
necessary.  This contradicts the assumption that only \(k\ge2\) sunny lines
are available.  Consequently, for every \(n\ge4\)

\[
k\in\{0,1\}.
\tag{8}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  The special case \(n=3\)

For \(n=3\) the set \(S_3\) consists of the six points  

\[
(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),\;(2,1),(2,2),\;(3,1).
\]

The three lines  

\[
L_{1}:y=x,\qquad
L_{2}:y=-\frac12x+\frac52,\qquad
L_{3}:y=-2x+5
\]

are all sunny and together contain the six points; therefore \(k=3\) is
realizable.

If we tried to use exactly two sunny lines, the three points
\((2,1),(2,2),(3,1)\) would again force the same obstruction as in
Section 5, showing that \(k=2\) is impossible.  Thus for \(n=3\)

\[
k\in\{0,1,3\}.
\tag{9}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Constructions for the admissible values  

* **\(k=0\).**  The \(n\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n\) are all
  non‑sunny and cover every point of \(S_n\).

* **\(k=1\).**  Take the \(n-1\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n-1\).
  The only uncovered point is \((n,1)\); the line through \((n,1)\) and
  \((1,2)\) has slope \(-\dfrac1{\,n-1\,}\neq0,\infty,-1\), hence it is
  sunny.  Exactly one sunny line is used.

* **\(n=3,\;k=3\).**  The three sunny lines displayed in Section 6 cover
  all six points of \(S_3\).

Thus every value listed in (8)–(9) is attainable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8.  Conclusion  

Combining the impossibility results of Sections 5 and 6 with the explicit
constructions of Section 7 we obtain the complete description of the
possible numbers of sunny lines.

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\text{If }n=3:\qquad k\in\{0,1,3\},\\[2mm]
&\text{If }n\ge4:\qquad k\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}}
\]
